Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on why he doesn't see an AI bubble bursting anytime soon, says ‘this time it’s different’
Article Text:
Jensen Huang says the world needs an entirely new layer of AI infrastructure

Jensen Huang says he is not worried about Nvidia customers spending on chips

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently said that he does not believe AI boom will end anytime soon, arguing that the current wave of spending is driven by a major shift in computing infrastructure rather than hype. Speaking in an interview with Axios co-founder Mike Allen, Jensen Huang said the AI industry is still in its early stages and demand for AI chips is backed by the need to build a new generation of computing systems. He said the semiconductor industry is not facing the kind of demand cycle that has led to previous boom-and-bust periods."The bubble will burst someday," he said, adding that it will not happen anytime soon because the AI infrastructure buildout is still in its early days."This time is different because this is not demand driven," Huang said during the interview. "This time is different because it's not seasonal. It's not demand driven means seasonal-demand driven. This is industrially driven, meaning the fundamental technology of computers is changing."Jensen Huang said the world now needs an entirely new layer of AI infrastructure, which will require far more chips than are being produced today.He estimated that the industry will need to become five to 10 times larger over the next decade.During the interview, Jensen Huang also dismissed concerns that heavy AI spending by major technology companies could become unsustainable. Several large cloud providers have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to build AI infrastructure, with some turning to the bond market to help fund those investments.Jensen Huang said he is not worried that Nvidia's customers are borrowing money to buy its chips because the shift to AI represents a long-term change in computing."So this future is a whole new way of doing computing that's fundamentally different than the past, and we need a lot more computers," he said.Huang added that AI is already generating profits for companies such as Anthropic as more customers adopt AI agents and other advanced tools. He described the technology as being at an "inflection point," where increased investment is helping improve productivity and expand AI adoption.He also argued that shortages of chips, land, electricity and construction workers are slowing the pace of expansion in a positive way, giving the industry more time to build the infrastructure needed before supply catches up with demand."We basically are constrained in every single direction, in every single way," Huang said. "That constraint is good. That constraint is what holds the system back. So that gives us plenty of time to go build out these infrastructure."
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says he is not worried about Nvidia customers spending on chips. He said the semiconductor industry is not facing the kind of demand cycle that has led to previous boom-and-bust periods. He estimated that the industry will need to become five to 10 times larger over the next decade.

Article Title: ‘How else are people going to learn’: MIT research scientist warns companies replacing Gen Z with AI for entry jobs risk a costly mistake
Article Text:
Andrew McAfee, a research scientist at MIT questioned how organisations expect future professionals to develop if entry-level jobs disappear.

Entry-level hiring plays a role in future workforce development

Young job seekers remain concerned about AI

Companies that replace Gen Z workers with artificial intelligence (AI) in entry-level roles could be creating long-term workforce challenges. Speaking to Harvard Business Review, Andrew McAfee, a research scientist at MIT and co-lead of the university's Initiative on the Digital Economy, questioned how organisations expect future professionals to develop if entry-level jobs disappear.“How else are people going to learn to do the job except via on-the-job learning and training apprenticeship? That’s how you learn to do difficult knowledge work is by helping somebody who’s good at that with the routine stuff. And when we put too much automation in that too quickly, we lose that apprenticeship ladder,” McAfee said.McAfee argued that reducing entry-level hiring does more than shrink the current workforce.He said it disrupts the pathway through which employees develop the skills needed for more complex roles over time.He also said companies risk losing a generation that is already comfortable working with artificial intelligence. According to a Deloitte study published in November 2025, 76% of Gen Z respondents reported using a standalone AI tool, the highest share among all generations.“There is a big demographic falloff. As people tend to get older, we tend to be more set in our ways and less willing to try crazy new things like AI,” McAfee, who is also the co-founder of Workhelix, said.“So if you’re pulling back on your entry-level hiring, you are probably sacrificing future opportunities to learn and the skilled people of the future. You’re also turning off the spigot of the most enthusiastic power users of AI in your organisation,” he added.McAfee's comments come as many graduates report growing concerns about the impact of AI on employment. According to Handshake's Class of 2026 Network Trends report, entry-level job postings on the platform are down 2% year over year and remain 12% below pre-pandemic levels.Meanwhile, the unemployment rate for college graduates aged between 22 and 27 stands at 5.6%, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.A Monster survey also found that nearly nine in 10 graduates from the Class of 2026 are concerned that AI or automation could replace entry-level jobs, compared with 64% in 2025.Some executives have echoed those concerns. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei had previously said AI could eliminate up to half of entry-level white-collar jobs before later softening that prediction.However, a recent Goldman Sachs analysis suggested younger workers have historically adapted more effectively to technological shifts. The report found college-educated young workers generally experience earnings losses around half as large as other displaced workers over the decade following job loss and are more likely to move into occupations that complement emerging technologies.“Contrary to current concerns that the costs of AI will fall especially hard on new graduates, younger workers have actually been able to adjust more flexibly through occupational mobility and skill upgrading in the past,” the report said.
Article Summary: Andrew McAfee, a research scientist at MIT, questioned how organisations expect future professionals to develop if entry-level jobs disappear. He said companies risk losing a generation that is already comfortable working with artificial intelligence. According to a Deloitte study published in November 2025, 76% of Gen Z respondents reported using a standalone AI tool.

Article Title: Mark Cuban predicts that in the AI age, much like race car drivers and pilots, future generations of workers will be trained using …
Article Text:
‘Training office workers like pilots and drivers’

“The next great AI application, driven by open source, or open weights, will be a job simulator.

How employees gain experience in a future AI world is going to be far different from today. Employees won’t have as many touch points in the company to gain knowledge and experience from. That’s where judgement has historically come from.

Much like race car drivers and pilots have software that is continually updated to enable them to experience as many scenarios as possible, trying to replicate what could happen IRL, smart companies will have their employees and stakeholders with the most domain knowledge create the simulator that takes them through every possible situation they could face and helps prepare them.

Onboarding will have a completely different meaning.”



AI will redefine corporate onboarding, says Cuban

Tech billionaire Mark Cuban has shared a bold prediction for the future of employment: as artificial intelligence (AI) changes traditional office workflows, companies will train incoming employees using immersive “job simulators. ” In a post on X on Thursday, former Shark Tank investor argued that traditional workplace onboarding, where junior employees gain judgment and domain knowledge by working with coworkers and hands-on experience, will soon be a thing of the past.To bridge the growing gap between entry-level hires and real-world experience, Cuban expects the “next great AI application” to be high-tech workplace simulation software.He compared the upcoming shift in corporate training to long-standing practices in aviation and motorsport.Commercial pilots routinely spend hundreds of hours in flight simulators to learn emergency protocols and flight mechanics safely on the ground. Similarly, race car drivers rely on ultra-realistic driving simulators to master track layouts, weather conditions and car mechanics without needing physical track access.Cuban noted that forward-thinking organisations will soon enlist their top experts to build these simulated environments."Smart companies will have their employees and stakeholders with the most domain knowledge create the simulator that takes them through every possible situation they could face and helps prepare them," Cuban explained, while adding, “Onboarding will have a completely different meaning.”
Article Summary: Tech billionaire Mark Cuban has shared a bold prediction for the future of employment. As artificial intelligence (AI) changes traditional office workflows, companies will train incoming employees using immersive ‘job simulators’ Cuban compared the upcoming shift in corporate training to long- standing practices in aviation and motorsport.

He noted that the partnership will help organizations “simplify operations, strengthen zero-trust enforcement, and deliver consistent, AI-powered protection at scale.”Raj Chopra, SVP & Chief Product Officer of Cisco’s Security Business Group, highlighted the need for simplification: “Enterprises don’t need another tool to stitch into an already complex security stack.They need a simpler way to secure how work actually happens across users, devices, applications, clouds, and increasingly AI agents.” Cisco Secure Access integrates identity context, zero trust, and AI-powered protection into one cloud-delivered platform, enabling consistent policy enforcement and seamless user experiences.The integrated SSE solution is designed to support enterprises as they step into the agentic era, offering robust protections for generative AI and AI agents. With end-to-end visibility, faster deployment, and streamlined modernization of security architecture, the partnership positions Tech Mahindra and Cisco as leaders in unified cloud security.By reinforcing resilience and simplifying secure access, the collaboration helps enterprises accelerate digital transformation in an increasingly distributed and AI-driven world. Article Title: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani is hiring software engineers, designers, researchers for his 'tech crew': Here's what the job actually is
Article Text:
NYC mayor wants his ‘tech crew’ to build city software from inside the agency



New York City is betting that in-house tech teams will ship faster and cost less



New York City has opened applications for a new kind of government job. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Monday that the city is recruiting software engineers, product designers, product managers, user researchers, service designers and data experts to staff what he is calling Public Interest Technology Crews—PIT Crews, a pun the mayor committed to by rolling up to the Coney Island go-kart track to make the announcement.The hiring is funded and specific. A City Hall spokesperson confirmed around 30 full-time roles across four crews, supported by $5.24 million in baseline funding in the mayor's new fiscal budget. The listings are live at nyc.gov/pitcrew.A PIT Crew is a mixed team—engineers, designers, product managers, user researchers and data experts—placed alongside staff at a city agency rather than parked in a separate technology department. The crew works with that agency and with New Yorkers to design, build and launch a digital tool, then learn from how people actually use it. The mayor's office describes the timeline as months rather than years, which is the entire premise of the model.Five crews are planned. One handles the Click to Cancel complaint portal, three are attached to Mamdani's affordability and public excellence agenda, and a fifth is being developed with support from The Rockefeller Foundation through the Mayor's Fund to Advance New York City.Zohran Mamdani’s PIT crew’s first assignment is a complaint portal with teethCrew one works with the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection on an online portal where New Yorkers can report companies that make subscriptions near-impossible to cancel. It supports the Click to Cancel rule Mamdani announced last week, which requires businesses to offer the same exit route customers used to sign up. Enforcement begins October 1, and the junk fees ban lands January 1, 2027.The portal is built to do two things at once—give individual New Yorkers a route to recourse, and give City Hall a running database of repeat offenders.Chief Technology Officer and OTI Commissioner Lisa Gelobter framed the roles around a shift in what government technology now is. Every service has a digital surface, she argued, and every confusing step in that surface erodes trust. Her operating instruction for the crews is user first, always, with outcomes weighted over outputs.There is a politics to the hiring as well. NYC-DSA's Tech Action organisers backed the announcement as a choice to build capacity inside government rather than route taxpayer money to consultancies and big tech vendors. BetaNYC's Noel Hidalgo made the cost version of the same argument—in-house teams that deliver faster and cheaper than the outsourced alternative."New Yorkers should not be forced to navigate systems that are confusing, outdated and burdened by bureaucracy," Mamdani said. "The PIT Crew turns that model on its head."Public Interest Technology took shape as a field in the 2010s on a fairly unglamorous premise: government software is usually bad, and fixing it is a staffing and usability problem more than an engineering one. The recruitment page leans into that, pitching the work rather than the salary—the goal, it says, is to make interacting with government dignified and delightful for every New Yorker.
Article Summary: New York City launches Public Interest Technology Crews (PIT Crews) Crews will build city software from inside the agency rather than in a separate department. Hiring is funded by $5.24 million in the mayor's new fiscal budget.

Article Title: Workplace software Monday.com cuts hundreds of jobs; read CEO Eran Zinman's 'layoff email' to employees
Article Text:
Here's the full memo sent by Eran Zinman, Co-founder and Co-CEO at Monday.com, to employees

Hi everyone,

Why are we making this change?

A flatter organization

More autonomous teams

A new go-to-market model

For the people leaving monday.com

For the people staying

We are deeply confident about our future

Israeli workplace software maker Monday.com is laying off hundreds of employees as part of a restructuring plan. The software company announced the layoffs in an Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing. The company said it is reducing its headcount by 20%, or about 630 staff, to “support a leaner, more focused operating model” as it concentrates on its AI Work Platform.In the SEC filing, the Tel Aviv-based company said that it has "initiated a restructuring plan." In a memo sent to employees about the layoffs, posted to LinkedIn, Eran Zinman, a cofounder of the company, claimed that the move was not about replacing employees with technology."We are not making this change to protect what we have. We are making it to go all in on what monday.com can become," the memo reads.Over the past nine months, we have shifted our core vision moving from managing work to doing the work for our customers, with people and AI agents working together in one workspace. This has required us to change our product, our strategy, and how we serve our customers.But it became clear that changing our strategy and product is not enough.The organization we built for our previous chapter is not the organization that fits the new AI era. Today, we are announcing the very difficult decision to reduce our global workforce by ~20%, affecting around 620 people.This is the most painful decision we have made since founding monday.com - yet we are certain it is the right one. We made it. We own it. And we take full responsibility for it.The people leaving are talented colleagues and friends. They helped build this company, support our customers, and create a culture we are deeply proud of. We are incredibly grateful to them, and we know that nothing we say can lessen the impact this will have on them and their families.We are not making this change to protect what we have. We are making it to go all in on what monday.com can become.We entered a new era where AI is transforming the role of software, creating the greatest opportunity our industry has ever seen.We have a new market to capture. Without a fundamental change in how we operate, we will not be able to compete and win that market.To fully realize this opportunity, and ensure monday.com is positioned to lead in this landscape, we need to move faster, execute more decisively, take on new challenges, respond quickly to market changes, and empower people in the company to create greater impact. Some of the things we are changing in monday:- We are reducing management layers, creating more empowered teams, and enabling faster decision-making.- We are moving from teams with many dependencies to smaller groups with broader ownership and greater authority to execute.- Our new offering is opening a new market, and that market requires us to work differently. New and existing customers increasingly expect deeper implementation support as they adopt AI. We will work more closely with customers, increase our on-site presence, create new roles, and adapt many existing ones.Improving margins was not the purpose of this decision. We intend to reinvest the vast majority of the savings in our people, our products, AI, and future growth.Thank you. Thank you for all your hard work, for the significant impact you have made, for caring so deeply about monday.com, and for always being willing to help and lend a hand. We know this is part of our culture, and it is something we consistently hear from everyone who interacts with people at monday.com.We want to be very clear: this decision is not a reflection of your performance, your contribution, or your value. It is the result of a management decision about how to structure the company for its next chapter.We are committed to supporting you through this transition with care, respect, and meaningful assistance. We will do everything we reasonably can to help you find your next opportunity, and we will provide you with a generous support package.To companies that are hiring: we recommend these people wholeheartedly. They are exceptional professionals and teammates, and we will help connect them with organizations looking for outstanding talent.It is not easy to be part of such a significant change or to see colleagues and friends leave so quickly. We understand how difficult this will be. We also owe you clarity about what this change means.The change is not about asking fewer people to do the same amount of work. We are making real choices about what we will stop doing. We will simplify how we work, remove unnecessary friction, and give teams more authority to make decisions.The company that comes out of this change will have clearer priorities, fewer layers, faster decisions, and greater ownership.Our path is very clear to us. This is a change we have chosen to make, and we are taking full responsibility for it. We have never seen such a significant opportunity in software, driven by such exciting technology.Nothing gives us more confidence than seeing how new and existing customers are responding to our new offering, and seeing adoption of our AI products accelerate.Every week, we see more evidence that our strategy is the right one. Customers are embracing our new vision, adoption of our AI capabilities continues to accelerate, and our confidence continues to grow.Our momentum is strong, and we believe we are on the right path to success on a massive market opportunity.To ease the uncertainty around this we will send all employees an email message within the next hour, followed by a personal call from one of your managers.For all managers - we know how difficult it is to process this personally, even as you continue to lead your teams. We have every confidence in your leadership and know you’ll approach these conversations with the care, clarity, and respect that define our culture. Thank you for being there for your people during this transition.Thank you,Roy & Eran
Article Summary: Israeli workplace software maker Monday.com is laying off hundreds of employees as part of a restructuring plan. The company said it is reducing its headcount by 20%, or about 630 staff, to “support a leaner, more focused operating model” as it concentrates on its AI Work Platform.

While availability may vary depending on hardware and location, reports confirm that more users outside beta programs are now seeing these updates.The combination of immersive navigation and a built-in speedometer reflects Google’s push to make Maps and Android Auto more driver-friendly and AI-powered. For users in India and globally, these updates promise smoother journeys, better situational awareness, and a glimpse into how Google is reshaping in-car experiences with AI integration.

Zandi said that America’s stubborn inflation problem is not a mystery but it’s the result of deliberate policy decisions. In a breakdown shared via a post on X (formerly known as Twitter) Zandi noted that inflation has run above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target for 64 straight months, with headline inflation at 3.5%. He also wrote that when you ‘net out the inflation tailwinds and headwinds, it’s clear the uncomfortably high inflation is the result of policy choices’. Zandi also said that the Americans are right to view high inflation and the increasing cost of living as their biggest financial challenge, and he argues that the roots of the problem lie in trade and immigration policies that have reshaped the economy.wrote Zandi.According to Zandi, two major policy decisions are directly adding to inflation: broad‑based tariffs and highly restrictive immigration laws. Zandi said tough immigration policies are steadily adding to inflation because they reduce the available workforce in essential sectors such as construction and agriculture. With fewer workers, labor shortages intensify, pushing wages and production costs higher — and those costs ultimately show up in consumer prices.He added that the Iran war and related energy surges have compounded these pressures. Without these policy‑driven hurdles, Zandi said inflation would have been 2.2% last year andthis year.said Zandi in a post on X.Zandi emphasized that underlying economic forces are actually leaning against inflation. A soft job market, moderating labor costs, rising vacancy rates, falling rents on new leases, and weak vehicle prices are all pushing inflation downward. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported a 0.4% drop in CPI in June 2026, the largest monthly decline since April 2020.But these natural disinflation trends are being overshadowed by policy choices that raise costs across the economy. Zandi’s conclusion is blunt:Zandi concluded.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos ex-wife MacKenzie Scott who sold half of her Amazon stake helped write a 'donation playbook' that Snap founder Evan Spiegel is following
Article Text: Snap co-founder Evan Spiegel and his wife, supermodel Miranda Kerr, recently made a multimillion-dollar donation that will wipe out $550 million in medical debt for over 261,000 Californians. Interestingly, this sophisticated philanthropic model was pioneered by MacKenzie Scott, Jeff Bezos ex-wife, who has donated more than $26 billion to over 2,700 non-profit organisations through her platform, Yield Giving. By leveraging a high-impact “donation playbook” to effective nonprofits, Spiegel is emulating the strategy that transformed Scott into the most prolific philanthropist of her generation.Snap founder Evan Spiegel is following the Scott modelThe donation was made to Undue Medical Debt, a nonprofit organisation that gained national prominence largely through early, substantial investments from MacKenzie Scott. The massive debt relief effort will target vulnerable residents across the state, with San Diego and Los Angeles counties receiving the largest shares of assistance.Scott donated a combined $80 million to the organization between 2020 and 2022, helping the once-scrappy nonprofit abolish over $40 billion in medical debt across all 50 states.Spiegel’s strategy mimics Scott’s signature approach: identify scalable organisations, provide massive, unrestricted capital, and leverage unique market opportunities for maximum impact.“The scale of this gift to Californians is truly astonishing, unburdening over a quarter million families of over half a billion dollars of un-payable medical debt,” said Allison Sesso, president and CEO of Undue Medical Debt.The unique way of abolishing medical debtThe mechanism that enables this exponential impact lies at the intersection of distressed debt markets and American healthcare dysfunction. Hospitals routinely sell uncollectible patient debt to collectors in bulk portfolios for pennies on the dollar. Undue Medical Debt enters this market as a bulk buyer, acquiring these portfolios at the same steep discounts. However, instead of trying to collect the money, the organisation permanently abolishes the debt.Starting in mid-July, eligible Californians began receiving letters informing them that their medical debt has been erased. The relief is targeted toward residents whose medical debt threatens access to essential care and economic stability.
Article Summary: Snap co-founder Evan Spiegel and his wife, supermodel Miranda Kerr, made a multimillion-dollar donation that will wipe out $550 million in medical debt for over 261,000 Californians. The donation was made to Undue Medical Debt, a nonprofit organisation that gained national prominence largely through early, substantial investments from MacKenzie Scott.

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes his first-ever post on Twitter; says: I am sharing a letter signed on why ...
Article Text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang joined Twitter in June this year

Here’s the full text of letter Jensen Huang shared in his first Twitter post



"In the 1980s, early open-source software pioneers challenged the prevailing belief that software would advance only if companies kept tight control over their code. This movement pushed for a transparent ecosystem where developers around the world could study, modify, and improve software. Software developed by the open-source community now supports most of the internet and underlies systems used by the world’s largest technology companies, as well as the U.S. military and federal agencies conducting scientific research, cybersecurity, and other critical missions. Open source did more than lower the cost of software; it created a shared foundation of knowledge on which generations of American engineers and entrepreneurs built their institutional sovereignty.

The United States now faces a similar choice with artificial intelligence. Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector. This is essential for creating opportunities for innovation and prosperity across the country. It requires expanding access to AI, encouraging competition, robust application layers, and giving Americans greater control over the technology they rely on. Open-weight models—AI models that anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure—are an important part of that foundation because they make advanced AI more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.

Open weights expand access to the AI economy. Startups, established businesses, universities, and public institutions can build on advanced models without training one from scratch or paying frontier model prices for every task. Open weights let every organization match the right model to the right job at the right cost, reserving frontier-scale capability for genuine frontier problems and running efficient, specialized models everywhere else. That discipline is what will make AI economically sustainable as its use scales into the billions of everyday tasks.

America

wins the AI era by diffusing it into the workflows of factories, hospitals, farms, classrooms, and main street businesses.

Open weights also strengthen competition and competition is what keeps the gains of AI broadly shared rather than concentrated in a few hands. By allowing many organizations to build, adapt, and deploy advanced models, open weights create rivalry not only among model developers but across cloud chips, applications, and services. That competition spurs innovation, drives down costs, and distributes the benefits of AI broadly across our economy. Open weights also give customers greater control. As organizations invest in AI, they want to know that they will not become locked into a single provider or lose the knowledge and capabilities they build over time. Open weight models help provide that assurance by allowing organizations to control their own data, evaluate and adapt models to their own needs, and deploy them wherever their business requirements demand. And as organizations create value with AI, open weights allow them to own that value through self-improving models, specialized capabilities, and accumulated knowledge that drive American sovereignty and prosperity.

To be sure, open weights carry real and distinct risks. Once released, the weights are beyond the original developer's control, and modified versions are difficult to trace or reverse. But the right response to this risk is not to prohibit open weights. In a world where cybersecurity attackers use advanced AI, defenders need access to models with comparable capabilities so they can detect, simulate, and respond to emerging threats. Open models broaden defensive capability, increase transparency, and allow vulnerabilities to be discovered and remediated across many teams.

In fact, openness may be one of the most important paths to AI safety and security. Relying solely on closed models is not inherently safe: they can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect. And concentrating advanced AI capabilities behind a small number of closed models compounds that risk. It results in a small number of single points of failure, weakens competition, and leaves critical technology in the hands of a few providers. Open weight models, on the other hand, allow a broad community of researchers and developers to examine their behavior, identify vulnerabilities, develop safeguards, and improve them over time. Just as open-source software demonstrated that transparency can be more secure than obscurity, AI safety may depend on giving more people the ability to test and strengthen the models on which society relies. It allows for rigorous benchmarking and evaluation, red teaming, and protections tied to real and demonstrated harms rather than assuming that closed systems are safer by default.

A strong AI ecosystem is not a foregone conclusion. Policymakers have an important opportunity to act. This includes expanding access to compute for startups and researchers, investing in shared training assets (datasets, tools, evaluation frameworks), and keeping the frontier plural by avoiding premature restrictions on open models that stifle competition or drive innovation overseas. These measures must also look at how strong application layers can expand sovereign use of AI across the economy.

In shaping this ecosystem, policymakers should be careful not to conflate legitimate model development techniques with misappropriation. Distillation, or the practice of using one model's outputs to help train or improve another, is a widely used technique for model improvement, evaluation, and validation. It reflects a long tradition of learning from, building upon, and improving existing technologies, a tradition that has helped drive innovation since the rise of the open-source software movement. By contrast, unlawful efforts to extract value from closed models raise legitimate concerns. Those concerns should be addressed through targeted legal and commercial frameworks rather than sweeping restrictions on techniques that play an important role in AI innovation.

The age of AI can be one of prosperity. With the right choices, open weight AI can expand opportunity, strengthen competition, extend American technological leadership, mitigate risk, and ensure that the benefits of this extraordinary technology are shared broadly across our economy. That future is worth building, and the United States should lead in building it."

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made his first-ever post on Twitter (now X) on July 24. In the post, Jensen Huang shared an open letter on why open models matter. The letter, signed by Nvidia and 24 other companies, warns the US not to repeat the mistake of over-restricting technology the way some feared for open-source software in the 1980s. It argues that open-weight AI models should be preserved as a foundation for American leadership. “Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector,” the letter says, adding “This is essential for creating opportunities for innovation and prosperity across the country”.Sharing the post, Jensen Huang wrote:“For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter. AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country.Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty. The world needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models."
Article Summary: Jensen Huang: U.S. will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector. It requires expanding access to AI, encouraging competition, robust application layers, and giving Americans greater control over technology.

Article Title: ‘Shortest day of 2026’ is set to come this month, though this tiny time change in Earth’s day may look ‘small’, how this 'milli-seconds shift' is threatening GPS and satellites
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representational purpose only

What is actually happening on July 26



Why Earth’s rotation changes



1.33 milliseconds per century: Climate change connection with GPS, space missions



This Sunday, July 26, will be the shortest day of 2026. However, the difference is so tiny – just 0.65 milliseconds – that no one will notice. This time is less than the blink of an eye, less than the time it takes a camera flash to fire, and life will carry on entirely undisturbed. But behind that ‘flicker of time’ lies a story that scientists say should concern all of us. The Earth's rotation is altering in ways that are unmatched in at least 3.6 million years, and climate change is the reason.According to the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service (IERS), the organisation responsible for keeping global time, Sunday's day will measure approximately 0.65 milliseconds shorter than the standard 24 hours, or 86,400 seconds. That makes it the shortest day of the year so far. But here is the thing: it is actually less extreme than recent years.In 2025, the shortest day, recorded on July 10, came in at 1.37 milliseconds shorter than standard. This year’s figure is roughly half that, suggesting Earth's recent spell of unusually rapid rotation may be easing. The data comes from TimeAndDate.com, which reported the IERS's mid-July predictions, and it tells a story of a planet whose rotation is shifting in ways that are small in the short term but significant over decades and centuries.Earth’s speed of rotation is not fixed. It fluctuates constantly due to a complex web of factors, including ocean currents, atmospheric pressure and the gravitational pull of the moon that shifts in how mass is distributed across the planet.Time on Earth is based on Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), which is designed to closely follow the planet’s rotation. When the rotation drifts significantly, timekeepers add or remove “leap seconds” to keep UTC aligned with the actual position of Earth.This is where the story becomes genuinely alarming and where a fraction of a millisecond starts to carry real weight. New research from the University of Vienna and ETH Zürich, published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth earlier this year, has found that Earth's day is currently lengthening at a rate of approximately 1.33 milliseconds per century. That rate is faster than anything seen in at least 3.6 million years of Earth’s history.As climate change melts glaciers and polar ice sheets, the water they contain moves from the poles toward the oceans, redistributing mass across the planet. Earth slows down when mass moves away from its rotational axis toward the equator.Researchers reached this conclusion by analysing fossil remains of benthic foraminifera and using advanced machine learning techniques to reconstruct how day length has changed over millions of years.Modern satellite navigation systems, including GPS, Galileo and GLONASS, depend on extraordinarily precise knowledge of Earth's rotation. When users ask the phone for directions or a pilot uses GPS to land a plane, the system is calculating the users’ position based on where Earth is pointing at any given millisecond. If Earth's rotation drifts faster than the models predict, those calculations drift too.Space missions face similar challenges. Navigating a spacecraft requires knowing exactly how Earth is oriented, which means errors of even a fraction of a millisecond in rotation data can translate into meaningful positional errors at the distances involved.Global timekeeping systems are also affected. The decision of when to add or remove a leap second depends on accurate tracking of Earth’s rotation. As the rate of change accelerates, those decisions become more complex and the margins for error shrink.The changes are currently manageable. But as the rate of lengthening continues, the pressure on the systems that underpin modern navigation, communication and timekeeping will grow.
Article Summary: Sunday, July 26, will be the shortest day of 2026. But the difference is so tiny – just 0.65 milliseconds – that no one will notice. But behind that ‘flicker of time’ lies a story that scientists say should concern all of us. The Earth's rotation is altering in ways that are unmatched in at least 3.6 million years, and climate change is the reason.

AI giant Anthropic, the creator of Claude model, is gearing up for one of the most closely watched IPOs of the year and it’s hiring accordingly as reported by Business Insider. As the company is preparing to go public as early as this fall, it has posted a new opening for a director of investor relations, offering a base salary between $425,000 and $600,000. The role will be central to shaping Anthropic’s pitch to public-market investors as it attempts to justify its $965 billion valuation, reported in May. As per the listing, the director will help craft Anthropic’s, act as a primary liaison between major investors and company leadership, and attend meetings to explain Anthropic’s products, strategy, and how key decisions could affect the stock.They will also track AI industry developments and work closely with Anthropic’s new head of investor relations, Kenneth Dorell, who joined in June after leading Meta’s IR team. The company confirmed that its previous IR lead, Vu Bui, departed earlier this year.Anthropic’s revenue has increased over the past year, driven by enterprise adoption of tools like Claude Code. In May, the company said its run-rate revenue had crossed $47 billion, cementing its position as OpenAI’s most significant competitor.But the company faces a tricky balancing act: AI labs are expensive to run, require massive capital for model training, and operate under unusual governance structures. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, legally required to balance shareholder returns with the long‑term safe development of advanced AI.The job listing even nods to this complexity, noting that preferred candidates should have anand enthusiasm for explaining a research‑driven company to financial audiences.Anthropic and OpenAI represent a new category of company for Wall Street — privately valued in the hundreds of billions, burning enormous sums on compute, and navigating intense government scrutiny. Their researcher communities also wield unusual influence over corporate direction. For guidance, Anthropic’s IR team can look to SpaceX, which went public at a $1.77 trillion valuation in June by positioning itself as a major AI player. After an initial surge, SpaceX shares later fell below their listing price — a reminder of how volatile investor sentiment can be in the AI sector.In related news, recently, Canada’s federal banking regulator has warned the country’s largest financial institutions about the risks posed by Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and other advanced AI systems, according to a report by Reuters. In an April email obtained by Reuters, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) cautioned that frontier AI models could increase cyber threats and compress the time banks have to identify and fix the vulnerabilities. The email, sent to chief technology, information security, and risk officers across Canada’s financial industry, outlined practices to enhance risk identification and response.OSFI wrote.Following Reuters’ inquiries, OSFI published a public bulletin emphasising its technology-neutral, risk-focused approach. The regulator said its concern is not the technology itself but how institutions govern and manage risks associated with its use.

Article Title: Bill Gates once dragged his rival software boss to traffic court instead of a business meeting: That competitor helped him stay out of jail and keep his license
Article Text:
He owned a green Porsche and drove it at 100 mph, but Bill Gates' radar detector was useless the day cops clocked him from a plane

The speeding habit that Bill Gates' radar detector couldn't fix

Hard Drive: Bill Gates and the Making of the Microsoft Empire

How Microsoft rival Seymour Rubinstein saved Bill Gates in traffic court

Why Bill Gates' slow diesel Mercedes failed to curb his speeding

Before he was one of the richest men alive, Bill Gates had a speeding habit that kept landing him in trouble. The Microsoft co-founder loved fast Porsches, drove them hard, and collected enough tickets that traffic cops became a regular fixture of his early years. At one point his driving record got bad enough to put his license—and reportedly his freedom—on the line.So Gates did something unusual. When Seymour Rubinstein, one of Microsoft's biggest competitors, showed up expecting a business meeting, Gates told him the meeting was moving to traffic court. Rubinstein, the founder of MicroPro and the man behind the hugely popular WordStar, ended up coaching his young rival on how to avoid jail time and keep his license.Gates's love of speed went back to Microsoft's earliest days. He owned a green Porsche 911 and pushed it constantly. During the company's move from Albuquerque to Seattle, he reportedly drove the Porsche past 100 mph and got caught more than once. One time his radar detector was useless—police were clocking his speed from an aircraft overhead.The traffic court episode is documented in, the 1992 book by James Wallace and Jim Erickson. Rubinstein arrived for what he thought was a normal Microsoft meeting, only to be told he was heading to court to watch Gates answer for his driving.Rubinstein wasn't just any competitor. WordStar was one of the first commercially successful PC applications, and he later claimed it held 72% of the word-processing market going into 1984. Microsoft had released Word for MS-DOS on September 29, 1983, putting the two men on a direct collision course.But they went back a long way. Rubinstein was about 21 years older than Gates and had signed an early OEM deal with Gates and Paul Allen during his IMSAI days. They talked often and traded advice. Gates wanted to fight his ticket on a technicality—owning a radar detector was legal, he argued, and he felt the officer had treated him unfairly for spotting it. Rubinstein knew that wouldn't fly with a judge. He told Gates to apologise, promise to bin the radar detector, and swear he'd stop speeding. Gates listened, and dodged the worst of it.Gates later tried engineering a fix. He bought a sluggish brown Mercedes diesel—no working radio, so he could think while driving—treating it as a self-imposed speed limiter and a test of discipline. It didn't work. Fortune reported in 1986 that he kept collecting tickets even in the slower car. The Mercedes eventually died from an engine failure tied to an oil oversight, and Gates went back to a Porsche capable of roughly 155 mph. The problem, it turned out, was never the car.
Article Summary: Gates's love of speed went back to Microsoft's earliest days. He owned a green Porsche 911 and pushed it constantly. During the company's move from Albuquerque to Seattle, he reportedly drove the Porsche past 100 mph and got caught more than once. One time his radar detector was useless—police were clocking his speed from an aircraft overhead.

Article Title: As Oracle loses $498 billion in less than 10 months, why credit rating agency S&P has identified Sam Altman's OpenAI as a 'key credit risk' for Larry Ellison's company
Article Text:
Why S&P calls OpenAI a 'key credit risk'

Why Oracle's credit rating was downgraded

Here’s what S&P said about OpenAI being a ‘key security risk’ for Oracle

Oracle has lost about $498 billion in market value in less than 10 months. Recently, credit rating agency S&P Global Ratings identified Sam Altman 's OpenAI as a "key credit risk" for the company. In a report explaining its decision to downgrade Oracle's credit rating, S&P said the software giant's aggressive push into AI infrastructure has made it increasingly dependent on a handful of large customers, with OpenAI standing out as the biggest concern. The agency estimates OpenAI accounts for roughly half of Oracle's $638 billion in remaining performance obligations (RPO), warning that if the ChatGPT maker is unable to meet its financial commitments, Oracle could be left with costly data centre leases and weaker cash flow.S&P said Oracle's AI infrastructure business now carries much higher risks than its traditional software business because it requires massive upfront investments in data centres, chips and long-term leases before generating returns.According to the agency, OpenAI represents around 50% of Oracle's $638 billion RPO, making the Microsoft-backed AI company one of Oracle's most important customers. As mentioned anove, S&P warned that OpenAI's ability to honour its contracts depends on continued growth in the AI industry, its ability to raise external funding and whether its AI models remain market leaders."If OpenAI were unable to pay Oracle, we believe Oracle could be left with massive data center leases that it might be unable to exit or have to re-lease to new tenants under less-favorable terms," S&P said.The agency added that it is monitoring OpenAI's financial commitments to data centre operators and chip makers as an indicator of its future financial strength.S&P lowered Oracle's long-term credit rating to 'BBB-' from 'BBB', saying it had underestimated both the scale of Oracle's AI investments and their impact on the company's financial profile.The agency expects Oracle's cloud infrastructure business to grow from 27% of revenue in fiscal 2026 to nearly 60% by fiscal 2028. While that supports future growth, S&P believes it also exposes Oracle to greater financial risk because AI infrastructure requires heavy spending before profits are realised.Oracle has guided capital expenditure of $90 billion to $95 billion for fiscal 2027, far above S&P's earlier estimate of $60 billion.The rating agency now expects Oracle's free operating cash flow deficit to widen to nearly $42 billion in fiscal 2027, compared with its previous forecast of negative $24 billion.OpenAI remains a key credit risk. We estimate that OpenAI makes up roughly half of the $638 billion in RPO. OpenAI’s ability to meet its contractual obligations and raise external financing will be contingent upon AI tailwinds continuing and its models being market leaders. If OpenAI were unable to pay Oracle, we believe Oracle could be left with massive data center leases that it might be unable to exit or have to re-lease to new tenants under less-favorable terms. As a proxy for OpenAI’s future prospects, we’re tracking OpenAI’s financial commitments to data center operators and chip makers to gauge its overall financial exposure and its market share among enterprise and consumers.
Article Summary: S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle's long-term credit rating to 'BBB-' from'BBB. S&P said Oracle's aggressive push into AI infrastructure has made it increasingly dependent on a handful of large customers. The agency estimates OpenAI accounts for roughly half of Oracle's $638 billion in remaining performance obligations.

Article Title: As Europe Scientists struggles with heatwave, scientists find alternative to air conditioning, including advances in materials that passively cool buildings
Article Text:
For representative purpose

Why air conditioning cannot be sustainable solution



Solution: Sending heat directly into space



As record-breaking heatwaves sweep across large areas of Europe and Asia, city planners and homeowners are searching for ways to stay cool. While air conditioning remains the go-to fix in nations like the US, Japan, and Australia, scientists warn that installing AC units in every home is an unsustainable trap. Researchers have now highlighted breakthroughs in passive cooling materials, including specialised paints, hydrogel films and radiative coatings, that can lower building temperatures without relying on electricity or overloading power grids.Cooling buildings already accounts for nearly 10% of global electricity consumption, according to a recent review published in Nature Reviews Clean Technology. By 2050, the electricity required to cool indoor spaces is projected to jump by 210%, with greenhouse gas emissions from air conditioning expected to triple.Beyond energy consumption, scientists point out three critical flaws with traditional air conditioning. The first is grid strain that will be caused by massive spikes in AC usage during extreme heatwaves. The second is heat ‘Vicious Loop’. Standard split-system AC units cool indoor rooms by extracting heat and dumping it outdoors.This raises ambient outdoor temperatures in cities, driving higher demand for even more air conditioning.The third is the economic gap. The report says that up to 100 million families across developing regions in India, Mexico, Indonesia, and Brazil will remain unable to afford AC units by 2040, despite having electrical access.“Air conditioning can be life-saving for people at high risk, but the technology has severe drawbacks. We need solutions that don't compound the problem,” explains Matthaios Santamouris, an architecture researcher at the University of New South Wales.Passive cooling technologies require minimal to no power, using advanced material design to regulate building temperatures. The options include automated sun-tracking blinds and window slats that are already common in commercial towers. However, the most promising breakthrough involves passive radiative cooling.This tech takes advantage of the "atmospheric window"—a specific spectrum of heat waves (8 to 13 micrometers) that can pass directly through Earth's atmosphere and escape into space.The first is radiative paints that are infused with microscopic silica and aluminum oxide spheres to scatter solar radiation. This reflects 97% of solar energy and lowers surface temperatures by around 5.26 degrees Celsius.The second solution is evaporative hydrogel films that absorb moisture at night and evaporate water during hot daytime hours while repelling heat. These are claimed to reduce direct sunlight surface temperatures by about 7 degrees Celsius.The researchers say that applying these high-tech coatings to roofs and exterior walls effectively turns whole structures into self-cooling units.“We really need to tackle this problem from different angles,” says urban climatologist Negin Nazarian. By blending advanced materials with smart design, cities can keep residents safe during extreme summer heatwaves without worsening the global climate crisis.
Article Summary: By 2050, the electricity required to cool indoor spaces is projected to jump by 210%, with greenhouse gas emissions from air conditioning expected to triple. Researchers have highlighted breakthroughs in passive cooling materials, including specialised paints, hydrogel films and radiative coatings.

Article Title: Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, Dell, IBM sign joint letter urging US to back open weight AI models: Openness may be one of the most important paths to AI safety
Article Text:
Twenty-five US tech companies want Washington to avoid premature restrictions on open-weight AI models. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google did not sign.

Why 25 American tech companies are defending open-weight AI models right now

Jensen Huang, Satya Nadella and Michael Dell take the argument to social media

OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are the names missing from the list

Twenty-five American technology companies, venture firms and open-source foundations signed a joint letter on Friday asking Washington to leave open-weight AI models alone, arguing that America's lead in artificial intelligence will be settled by how far the technology spreads rather than by who builds the single best model. Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, Dell Technologies, IBM, Palantir, Mistral, Mozilla, the Linux Foundation, Hugging Face, Andreessen Horowitz and Y Combinator are among the names on it.The letter lands in the middle of a fight. The letter arrives while senior Trump administration officials weigh action against Moonshot AI, the Chinese startup whose Kimi K3 model has beaten American systems on several benchmarks this month. The signatories want policymakers to avoid "premature restrictions" that would, in their words, stifle competition or push innovation overseas. Their broader claim is sharper still: openness may be one of the most important paths to AI safety and security, not a threat to it.Open-weight models are the ones anyone can download, inspect, modify and run on their own servers. The letter argues that closed models are not automatically safer, since they can be breached or fail in ways nobody outside the company can see.Concentrating frontier capability behind a handful of providers, the signatories write, creates a small number of single points of failure.The letter also leans on history, drawing a straight line from the open-source software movement of the 1980s to today's argument. Mozilla and the Linux Foundation, two survivors of that era, both signed.Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang used his first-ever post on X to share it, writing that open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity while enabling sovereignty. Microsoft's Satya Nadella framed it as a path that protects national security rather than weakening it. Michael Dell said long-term leadership needs choice across the full ecosystem.Elon Musk, whose AI business sits under SpaceX, backed the letter without signing it. "This has my full support," he posted.The three biggest closed-model developers in the US stayed out. Both OpenAI and Anthropic are valued near $1 trillion and have confidentially filed for IPOs that could land this year. Both would benefit if Washington restricted Chinese open models. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman still posted that he was glad to see the letter and wants the US to win in open source and proprietary models alike.The unresolved fight is distillation, the practice of training a smaller model on a stronger one's outputs. White House OSTP director Michael Kratsios accused Moonshot on Wednesday of building Kimi K3 by distilling Anthropic's Fable 5. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went further on Tuesday, comparing it to theft and raising the prospect of sanctions.The letter defends distillation as a normal development technique while conceding that unlawful extraction from closed models is a real problem. Its fix is narrower than a ban. Those cases, it says, belong in targeted legal and commercial frameworks rather than sweeping rules that catch legitimate research in the same net.
Article Summary: Twenty-five US tech companies want Washington to avoid premature restrictions on open-weight AI models. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google did not sign. The letter arrives while senior Trump administration officials weigh action against Moonshot AI, the Chinese startup whose Kimi K3 model has beaten American systems on several benchmarks.

Article Title: One of the popular content creator platforms Patreon lays off 20% employees, CEO says ‘AI not the reason for job cuts’: Read note sent to workers
Article Text:
Patreon lays off 20% employees

Read email that Patreon CEO sent to employees



Hi Team,

I have a painful update this morning. I have decided to reduce the size of our team by 20%, or 93 people. All teammates at the company will receive an email within the next few minutes indicating whether or not your role is impacted by this change.

I’ll get into the reasons for this decision and logistics for the day below, but before I do, I want to acknowledge how painful this will be for the kind, ambitious, hard working, and mission-driven humans who make up this company. The people at Patreon are the core of our spirit and what makes our culture and business so special. Today will be hard for so many people, and as the person responsible for this decision and the decisions leading up to this, I don’t take that lightly. Please take the time you need today to support our departing teammates and yourself.

What’s changing and why

There are two key changes we are making today:

A workforce reduction

Changing our organizational structure and how we work

I’ll explain each below.

1. The workforce reduction

Nothing about our core business has changed – it remains strong and consistent:

More than 300,000 creators in nearly every country in the world are earning money on our platform.

Creators are earning billions of dollars each year on Patreon, and those earnings have continued to exhibit steady, strong growth.

Creators, members, revenue, and processing volume continue to show strong, consistent growth every month.

On top of that, our transformation to becoming a media and community network is starting to work:

Our network is now sending 1.5M new members to creators every month.

Creators have added ~200M free memberships over the past 3 years.

Feed-attributed memberships are up more than 5X since our network launch.

But our transformation is going to take time. We are setting our sights on massive problems: the attention economy is optimizing for addiction instead of long term relationships. Creators are finding it increasingly difficult to reach their followers and build strong communities. The legacy social platforms are locking creators into their systems instead of giving them independence. There is no company better positioned than Patreon to tackle these problems.

At the same time, the market in which we operate has undergone profound change over the last 6 months. We need to adjust our cost structure to ensure that we remain a stable, dependable rock for our creators as we work toward our long term ambition. The changes we're making today are painful, but they're necessary to ensure that Patreon can take the time we need to address the above problems from a position of strength.

2. Changing our organizational structure and how we work

We’re making a number of changes to our organizational structure and how we work. Specifically, we’re flattening the organization, refocusing teams on our top priorities, and evolving key aspects of our operations to make us faster at adapting to change.

We’re making those changes because with a smaller team, we need a new organizational structure to continue executing effectively on our strategy and priorities, which are not changing. We remain focused on:

Improving core creator and fan experiences on the platform, and

Helping creators grow their audiences and businesses through our network

In addition, I want us to have increased agility as a company. AI has fundamentally transformed the tech industry, the pace of change has never been more intense, and I expect it to get even faster. Each of us will play a role in redefining how we work together as the nature of our work continues to change over time.

AI is not a replacement for human creativity

One of the most discussed questions over the last few months has been whether AI is replacing humans.

To be clear about the impact of AI on today’s decision: we are not making the above changes because we believe AI replaces humans.

The more we have learned to use these new tools, the clearer it has become that they are not substitutes for the creativity, judgment, detail orientation, or craftsmanship that our teammates have in spades, nor do they replace the desire for human connection that all of us cherish so deeply. That’s my personal opinion, but more importantly, it’s the foundation of Patreon’s strategy: our product vision and business are both predicated on the value of human creativity and human connection.

AI has fundamentally transformed the tech industry, though, including how we work, how we build products, how we communicate, and more. That does have an impact on how we operate and organize.

Logistics for Today

To our teammates leaving:

In the email you receive from our People team, you’ll find details about next steps, severance packages, and information about how to connect with a member of the People team if you have any questions. You’ll also receive a separate message from a member of our senior leadership team inviting you to a personal call if you would like.

You'll have access to your Patreon laptop and Slack through 5PM PT today. Access to all other internal systems will be removed, because we want to ensure we protect our creators and their businesses.

I know how important it is for folks to be able to say goodbye, so we've created a #gratitude-and-farewell

Slack channel

as a place for all of us to connect, if you feel comfortable.

Severance details:

We’ve prepared a severance package to support impacted employees through this transition:

16 weeks of pay starting from today, including remaining on payroll through our August 20th vesting date.

One additional week of pay for every full year worked at the company.

Additional cash payment to accommodate a) recent hires who haven’t reached their 1-year cliff, and b) more-tenured teammates who haven’t yet received their 2026 refresh grant.

Healthcare

coverage through the end of the year for eligible employees and families.

A $1,500 stipend to replace your company laptop.

Thank you for everything you’ve given our creators, fans, and this company. Your contributions have made a massive difference in the lives of so many people, and I’m deeply grateful for the energy, craft, and care you’ve put into your work. That work is now a part of Patreon and will continue to benefit creators and their communities for years to come.

To our teammates remaining:

The focus for today will be on our departing teammates, but we’ve scheduled a short video call for those of us remaining to be together as a team. Tomorrow, we’ll have an all hands and Q&A to review the details of the reorganization and changes to how we work. Next week, we’ll get together in person as planned to dive deeper on our H2 plans.

For over a decade, Patreon has been growing and evolving to ensure that creators are properly compensated for the value they create in the world. We have successfully adapted and thrived through recessions, the chaos of online media, and multiple market shifts. We continue to come out the other side stronger than before, and that’s exactly what we’ll do again.

Patreon, a popular creator subscription platform, is laying off 20% of its workforce, cutting roughly 93 positions as part of a broader corporate restructuring. The move was first reported by 404 Media and subsequently confirmed in a company-wide memo sent by Patreon CEO Jack Conte. Addressing concerns over the role of automation in the cutbacks, Conte explicitly stated that the job eliminations were not driven by artificial intelligence (AI) replacing human workers, though he acknowledged that AI has fundamentally altered the technological landscape.Conte reassured creators that Patreon’s core business remains “healthy and strong” and that its primary subscription model will not change.He said that the workforce reduction is aimed at streamlining internal management and redirecting resources toward high-priority features. The company is reducing layers of middle management to speed up decision-making, and making changes in key product operations to make the company faster at adapting to market changes.
Article Summary: Patreon CEO sent an email to employees saying the company is reducing its team by 20%. The company is also changing its organizational structure and how it works. The company says the changes are necessary to address problems in the social network. The email was sent to all employees.

Microsoft has responded to customer complaints over LG's Monitor App Installer. The software giant has asked the South Korean company to remove McAfee promotional pop-ups from the app. Confirming the move with a post on the microblogging site X (formerly Twitter), Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's Executive Vice President of Windows and Devices, said LG has agreed to disable the McAfee pop-up as an immediate step after reports that the app was being installed through Windows Update on some PCs connected to LG monitors.Responding to the issue on social media, Pavan Davuluri wrote,Davuluri's response came after a user shared a screenshot of the pop-up and wrote on X,Commenting on the post, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney tagged Davuluri and wrote,Replying to Sweeney, Davuluri wrote:The response comes after users reported that LG's Monitor App Installer appeared on their Windows systems following monitor driver updates and displayed a McAfee free trial advertisement. While LG said McAfee isMicrosoft said it has worked with the company to improve the experience for shared customers.The statement came days after users raised concerns on Reddit and YouTube, where several reports claimed LG's Monitor App Installer was automatically installed through Windows Update and repeatedly displayed advertisements for a 30-day McAfee trial.The issue gained attention after Reddit users reported that connecting certain LG monitors resulted in Windows silently installing the LG Monitor App Installer. According to user reports, the application later displayed McAfee advertisements during system startup.YouTube channel Gamers Nexus also reproduced the behaviour on an LG UltraGear 34GX900A-B monitor, reporting that the McAfee pop-up appeared on most system boots during testing. In addition to McAfee, the publication reported occasionally seeing promotions for LG Switch, LG Calibration Studio, LG Dual Controller and LG Channels.Microsoft documentation for device metadata notes that companion apps linked to hardware devices can be installed automatically when compatible devices are connected to a Windows PC under certain conditions.Although Microsoft confirmed the McAfee advertisement will be removed, reports noted that concerns remain over the automatic installation of companion apps through Windows Update.According to Microsoft's developer documentation, Universal Windows Platform (UWP) device apps can automatically install when supported hardware is connected to a Windows PC if certain setup requirements are met.The documentation also states,Similar automatic companion app installations have previously been reported for hardware from companies including Razer, Logitech, Asus and Gigabyte.Users who already have LG Monitor App Installer installed can remove it by going to Settings > Apps > Installed apps, locating the app and uninstalling it from Windows.
Article Summary: Microsoft has responded to customer complaints over LG's Monitor App Installer. Article Title: 150-plus Silicon Valley companies have sent a letter to the US government urging not to shut Chinese AI models; warn: Hundreds of American companies will instantly die
Article Text:
Nearly 200 Silicon Valley companies have asked the Trump administration not to cut off US access to Chinese open-weight AI models.

Startup founders say a Chinese AI ban would hand the market to Anthropic and OpenAI

White House escalates rhetoric on Moonshot AI even as blanket ban talk cools

Open-weight AI models expose a growing split between US labs and startups

Nearly 200 Silicon Valley companies, Proton and Y Combinator among them, have written to the Trump administration asking it not to cut off American access to Chinese open-weight AI models. The letters went out Wednesday from the newly formed Little Tech Association, addressed to President Donald Trump, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios. It is the first time the wider startup community has organised itself around this fight, and the timing is not accidental.The trigger was Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion-parameter open-weight model that landed last week and immediately dragged chip stocks down with it. Reports that Washington was weighing a ban on Chinese models followed within days. For founders who build on those models because they cannot afford to spend heavily on credits from Anthropic or OpenAI, the prospect reads less like national security policy and more like an extinction event.Suhail Doshi, founder of AI infrastructure startup Particle and a member of the association, put it without decoration. "There'll be hundreds of companies that instantly die," he told POLITICO."It's great for Anthropic. We're all going to have to spend money on Anthropic."That is the core of the argument. The letter says American leadership needs two things at once: world-leading US open-weight models, and continued access for American builders to open models already circulating globally. Blocking downloads, the founders write, would not slow the spread of Chinese models anywhere else in the world. It would only make US startups poorer and slower.Little Tech Association Executive Director Harry Godfrey wants targeted safeguards rather than blanket prohibitions. "A scalpel rather than a sledgehammer," he said, adding that the question policymakers should be asking is which approach addresses real security concerns without raising costs or limiting access.The administration is not committing either way in public. White House spokesperson Liz Huston said the US leads the world in AI innovation and Trump intends to keep it that way. A White House official, speaking anonymously, was blunter about the leaks: any policy announcement will come directly from the administration, and everything until then is speculation.Senior White House and Cabinet members did discuss the matter Monday night, according to two people familiar with those conversations. But a blanket ban was reportedly never seriously on the table. As of Wednesday, the Commerce Department had not drafted plans to add Chinese AI companies to its Entity List.The rhetoric has kept escalating regardless. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that the US could sanction Chinese firms found to have improperly distilled American models, citing watermarks from American systems turning up inside Chinese ones. Kratsios went further on Wednesday, alleging Moonshot distilled Anthropic's Fable model while building K3 using a purpose-built internal platform designed to evade detection, and that it acquired Nvidia GB300 servers despite a ban on their sale to Chinese entities. Moonshot has said nothing publicly.Kratsios was careful to say the administration supports open-source frameworks and open-weight models, drawing a line between ordinary distillation and industrial-scale theft. But the fight underneath is about who gets to build.Anthropic has spent months pushing for tighter restrictions on Chinese developers on security grounds. The startups signing this letter say restrictions do nothing to stop proliferation abroad and everything to raise costs at home. Kimi K3's full weights go up on July 27, free to download and modify. Whatever Washington decides after that, it will be deciding late.
Article Summary: Startup founders say a Chinese AI ban would hand the market to Anthropic and OpenAI. The trigger was Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion-parameter open- weight model. Proton and Y Combinator among them, have written to the Trump administration.
