ChatGPT is at the centre of a new lawsuit filed against its developer OpenAI by a Florida pastor. The latest lawsuit alleges that the AI chatbot repeatedly advised him to ignore worsening medical symptoms before he suffered a life-threatening pulmonary embolism (lung artery blockage). According to the complaint, ChatGPT allegedly drew on his Christian faith during their conversations, telling him, “God did not design your body to endlessly fail,” while encouraging him to trust that his symptoms would improve rather than seek emergency medical care.According to a report by the New York Post, the lawsuit, which was filed in San Francisco Superior Court by 55-year-old pastor Scott Winters, claims ChatGPT-4o spent months acting as an unlicensed physician by diagnosing his condition, recommending medications and treatment plans, and repeatedly assuring him that hospitalisation was unnecessary. Winters alleges he followed the chatbot's guidance, remained largely confined to a recliner for weeks and later suffered a massive pulmonary embolism caused by blood clots in both lungs.According to the complaint, Winters initially used ChatGPT as a research tool before it gradually became his primary source of medical advice. The lawsuit alleges the chatbot reviewed his medical records, interpreted laboratory reports and X-rays, diagnosed him with dysautonomia, recommended supplements and prescription medications, and developed personalised treatment plans without directing him to licensed healthcare professionals.The complaint states that after Winters reported recurring dizziness and unstable blood pressure, ChatGPT allegedly told him,Instead, it allegedly advised him to continue hisand avoid excessive movement until he experienced “8-10 more ‘episodes.'”The lawsuit further claims that hours before his medical emergency last year, Winters asked ChatGPT whether tenderness in his groin meant he should visit a hospital. According to the complaint, the chatbot responded that the pain wasrequiring immediate medical attention.Doctors later told Winters that the pulmonary embolism was likely caused by prolonged immobility, the lawsuit alleges.The complaint alleges ChatGPT incorporated Christian language into its responses, describing Winters' illness as part of a spiritual journey. It allegedly told him toassured him that “God was in the storm,” and described his recovery efforts as “a form of worship.”The lawsuit also claims the chatbot discouraged advice from others. After members of his church questioned why he was not seeking medical treatment, ChatGPT allegedly told Winters he was doing somethingby staying home and suggested others did not understand his condition.When his wife, a registered nurse, urged him to follow doctors' recommendations, the complaint alleges the chatbot characterised her advice asthatThe lawsuit alleges ChatGPT illegally practised medicine by diagnosing illnesses and recommending treatments without a medical licence. Winters is seeking damages and court orders requiring OpenAI to strengthen medical safeguards, suspend consumer-facing healthcare products until independent safety audits are completed, and permanently withdraw GPT-4o from the market.Responding to the allegations, an OpenAI spokesperson told The New York Post,the spokesperson said.The lawsuit comes weeks after another complaint filed in the same court alleged ChatGPT encouraged the suicide of a 29-year-old Alabama accountant by reinforcing delusional beliefs.OpenAI has denied the allegations in that and other pending lawsuits, saying ChatGPT is designed to recognise signs of emotional distress, encourage users to seek professional help and that the company continues to strengthen its safeguards with input from medical and mental health experts.
Article Summary: ChatGPT is at the centre of a new lawsuit filed against its developer OpenAI by a Florida pastor. The lawsuit alleges that the AI chatbot repeatedly advised him to ignore worsening medical symptoms before he suffered a life-threatening pulmonary embolism. The complaint alleges ChatGPT incorporated Christian language into its responses, describing Winters' illness as part of a spiritual journey.

Article Title: Andrej Karpathy who coined the term Vibe Coding shares user tips for writing better AI prompts
Article Text:
‘Let AI do the organising’



Read Karpathy’s full post on X (formerly Twitter):



One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos.

..". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

Andrej Karpathy, the prominent artificial intelligence (AI) researcher who famously coined the term “vibe coding,” has a piece of advice for anyone spending hours crafting the “perfect” text prompt for AI: stop trying so hard. Instead of typing out neat, polished instructions, Karpathy suggests users of AI chatbots should simply open the microphone and ramble.In a post on X, the former OpenAI and Tesla executive, who is now a leading AI researcher at Anthropic, revealed that his go-to prompting strategy involves turning on voice mode and talking continuously at a large language model (LLM) for nearly 10 minutes at a time.“Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve,” Karpathy wrote, describing his rambling voice sessions as a “total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness.”According to Karpathy, rambling aloud creates a far better division of labour between human intuition and machine processing power. He said that speaking allows humans to quickly dump every half-formed thought, nuance and goal without getting stuck on phrasing or grammar.The AI takes the chaotic monologue and organises it into clear, actionable and structured outputs. He added that by providing maximum context upfront, users “improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.”
Article Summary: Andrej Karpathy, the AI researcher who coined the term ‘vibe coding,’ suggests users of AI chatbots should simply open the microphone and ramble. He said that speaking allows humans to quickly dump every half-formed thought, nuance and goal without getting stuck on phrasing or grammar.
